title: What the long story teaches
hookLine: faith kept through exile, loss and renewal

lines: A MAN AND A MUSICIAN, WALKING.
cards: Stand at the end of a long road and look back, and you can't see every step. You see the shape. A man with a musician beside him, walking from village to village.
Towns built around a pool and a kitchen. Gurus who gave their lives rather than give way. A morning when five stood up.
Hard years in the hills and forests. A kingdom won and lost. Marches with no weapons.
A land split in two. A temple attacked, and grief in the streets. Families scattered across oceans, building gurdwaras in rented halls.

teach.b: The losses are real, and this story doesn't pretend. There were Gurus tortured and killed, families driven from their homes, sacred places damaged, and friends who never came back. Sikhs say those names out loud.

In the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh services, the sangat recalls those who gave their lives and kept their faith: who were cut limb from limb, broken on wheels, sawn apart, and who kept their Sikhi with their uncut hair to the last breath.
The losses are carried, standing, every day. And after every hard chapter, something kept going. The Granth kept being read.
The kitchen kept cooking. The gurdwara door kept opening, in a village in Punjab, a river town in Malaysia, a rented hall in a northern winter.
Sikhs often tell it this way: the faith didn't go on by winning every fight, but by keeping its daily practices.

teach.h: CHARDI KALA, AND THE GOOD OF ALL.
teach.b: The Ardas ends with this line: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Through the Name, rising spirits, and by your will, the good of all.
Chardi kala is the word for that spirit: rising, steady, even in loss. And notice what it asks for at the very end.
Not victory. The good of all. As the Ardas holds it: remember everything, keep the practice, and keep asking good for everyone.

how: In the Ardas, said standing at the close of Sikh services and at other moments, the sangat remembers the Gurus and the Sikhs who gave their lives for their faith, and ends by asking for chardi kala through the Name and the good of all.

o: a festival day of music and colored lights
a victory won after a long and hard fight
rising spirits, steady and hopeful even in loss

games.q: the road and its lesson — tap the pairs.
p: remembers those who kept their faith
kept cooking after every hard chapter

s: the Sikh story is told as one victory after another
the losses are real and named out loud in the Ardas: Gurus killed, families driven out, places damaged.
the Ardas ends by asking for the good of all
nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala: rising spirits through the Name, and the good of all.
the faith lasted because it won every fight
as Sikhs often tell it, it lasted by keeping its daily practices: the Granth read, the kitchen cooking, the door open.

games.q: after a terrible loss, the sangat gathers to say the Ardas. at the end, what does it ask for?
o: revenge on those who did it.
rising spirits through the Name, and the good of all.
games.why: nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. the losses are remembered, and the prayer still asks good for everyone.

practice: Let the year's stories pass in front of you like a slow train, the musician, the five, the marches, the kitchens, without holding on to any of them.
Let one stop, the one that stayed with you most, and as you breathe out, name quietly one thing it taught you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Chardi kala. Rising spirits, the steady, hopeful spirit asked for through the Name, kept through a faith's exile, loss and renewal. Today's word.

orig.note: chardi kala, rising spirits: the steady, hopeful spirit the Ardas asks for through the Name.

carryVoice: Your line: the lesson of the story. One lesson, named, is plenty. See you tomorrow.
